pages.name: Thrown up
pages.text: A ball is thrown straight up at 19.6 m/s. With no gravity it would rise `19.6t` metres in `t` seconds, its [[straight-line part]], but gravity pulls it `4.9t²` below that line, its [[squared part]]. Its height `h` is the gap between the two, so slide the time and watch it open and close.

pages.alt: Ball. A graph against time of 19.6t, where it would be with no gravity, and 4.9t², gravity's pull. The gap between them, drawn up from the axis, makes an upside-down U. At 1 s the gap is 14.7 m.

pages.name: When it lands
pages.task: When does the ball land back on the ground?
pages.why: It lands when the gap closes, where `19.6t = 4.9t²`. Taking out `4.9t` gives `4.9t(4 − t) = 0`, so 0 s, the throw, or 4 s, the landing.

pages.name: Roots and top
pages.text: The gap closes where the two parts are equal, `19.6t = 4.9t²`, which is `4.9t(4 − t) = 0`. So it is zero at 0 s, the throw, and 4 s, the landing, the two [[roots]]. The top sits halfway, at 2 s, `39.2 − 19.6 = 19.6` m, the same digits as the speed only because of the speed chosen.

pages.name: Off the deck
pages.task: Now a ball is thrown up at 4.9 m/s from a deck 9.8 m above the water, example figures. When does it hit the water?
pages.why: Set the parts equal, `9.8 + 4.9t = 4.9t²`, and divide by 4.9 to get `t² − t − 2 = 0`. That is `(t − 2)(t + 1) = 0`, so 2 s or −1 s, and −1 s is before the throw.

pages.name: A battery and a load
pages.text: A 12 V battery with 0.5 Ω inside it makes `12I` watts at a current `I`, its straight-line part, and burns `0.5I²` of that inside, its squared part. The load gets the gap, `P`. Each load lets through its own current, so sliding the current is choosing the load: the gap closes at 0 A, nothing connected, and at `12 ÷ 0.5 = 24` A, a short circuit.

pages.name: The best current
pages.task: What current gives the load the most power?
pages.why: The gap is zero at 0 A and 24 A, and a parabola is the same either side of its middle. So the most power is halfway, at 12 A, where the load gets `144 − 72 = 72` W.

pages.alt: Supply. A graph against current of 12I, the power the battery makes, and 0.5I², the power lost inside it. The gap between them, drawn up from the axis, makes an upside-down U.

pages.name: The most power
pages.text: The most power sits halfway between the roots, at 12 A, where the load gets `144 − 72 = 72` W. The load then has 6 V across it, so its resistance is `6 ÷ 12 = 0.5` Ω, the same as the battery's `r`. This is [[maximum power transfer]], and half of the 144 W made is lost inside.

pages.name: Double the load
pages.task: At 12 A the load is 0.5 Ω. Double it to 1 Ω. What power does the load get now?
pages.why: The load and the battery's 0.5 Ω are in series, 1.5 Ω in all, so the current falls to `12 ÷ 1.5 = 8` A and the load gets `8² × 1 = 64` W, which is also `96 − 32` on the curve at 8 A. That is less power, but 64 W of the 96 W made, about two-thirds, where at 12 A it was half: power traded for less lost.

pages.name: A loaded beam
pages.text: A 6 m beam on two simple supports carries 2 kN on every metre, so each support pushes up 6 kN. Taking turning effects about a point `x` metres along, and counting only what lies to its left, so not the right support's grey push, the left push turns the beam `6x` kN·m one way, and the `2x` kN of load on those metres, acting at their middle, turns it `2x × x ÷ 2 = x²` the other. The [[bending moment]] `M` is the gap, so drag the point and watch it close at both supports.

pages.name: Largest moment
pages.task: What is the largest bending moment in the beam?
pages.why: The bending moment is zero at both supports, 0 m and 6 m, so it is largest halfway, at 3 m. There `M = 18 − 9 = 9` kN·m, matching `wL²/8 = 2 × 6² ÷ 8 = 9`.

pages.task: Here is a worked answer for when the deck ball reaches its top. Which line slips?
pages.why: The top is halfway between the rule's two roots, −1 s and 2 s, so at `(−1 + 2) ÷ 2 = 0.5` s, even though −1 s is thrown away as a time. Line 2 goes halfway from the throw to the water, which only works when they are at the same height.

pages.task: A 4 m beam on two simple supports carries 3 kN on every metre, example figures. What is its largest bending moment?
pages.why: Each support holds half of the 12 kN, 6 kN, so `M = 6x − 1.5x²`. That is zero at 0 m and 4 m, so it is largest at 2 m, `12 − 6 = 6` kN·m, matching `3 × 4² ÷ 8 = 6`.
